title: Are there practical applications of the generalized divisibility theorem

problemStatement.formal: For base b, modulus d with b % d = 1: digitsum_b(a) + digitsum_b(c) ≡ digitsum_b(a+c) (mod d) and digitsum_b(a) * digitsum_b(c) ≡ digitsum_b(a*c) (mod d)
problemStatement.plain: Digit sums respect both addition and multiplication modulo d when b % d = 1, enabling arithmetic verification (casting out nines and generalizations).

proven: digit_sum_add_general: digit sums respect addition mod d (general)
digit_sum_mul_general: digit sums respect multiplication mod d (general)
detect_add_error_general: contrapositive error detection for addition
detect_mul_error_general: contrapositive error detection for multiplication
Specializations: casting out nines (mod 9), threes (mod 3), sevens (octal), fifteens (hex)
knownResults.goal: Complete formalization of casting out nines and generalizations

currentState.focus: Formalized casting out nines and generalizations

knowledge.progressSummary: COMPLETED: 229-line Lean file with 17 theorems, 0 axioms, 0 sorries. Formalizes casting out nines for addition and multiplication, general casting out for arbitrary base/modulus, error detection contrapositives, and concrete examples.
builtItems: src/data/proofs/divisibility-by-3-oq-04/ (gallery entry with meta.json, annotations.json, index.ts)
insights: Digit sums form a ring homomorphism N -> Z/dZ when b % d = 1
Nat.add_mod and Nat.mul_mod provide the algebraic transfer through arithmetic operations
Error detection is a simple contrapositive - no false positives but false negatives for multiples of d
Casting out threes catches 2/3 of errors vs 8/9 for nines - tradeoff between detection rate and simplicity
nextSteps: Could formalize alternating digit sum rule for divisibility by b+1 (e.g. 11 in base 10)
Could formalize digital root (iterative digit summing)
